common_name: Night Sky Petunia (Deep Purple Starry White-Speckled Petunia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Night Sky's speckled pattern varies from flower to flower and shifts with temperature, showing fewer white flecks in hot weather and a more heavily speckled look in cooler conditions.

directions: Night Sky became an overnight sensation for its deep violet-purple flowers randomly speckled and streaked with white, giving each bloom a starry-night appearance unlike any solid-colored petunia, with no two flowers marked exactly alike. The pattern is temperature-sensitive, appearing with fewer white speckles during hot weather and more pronounced flecking as temperatures cool in spring and fall, adding an extra layer of seasonal variation to an already novel bloom. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and deadhead or shear back by half in midsummer if the mounded, spreading habit becomes leggy, which encourages fresh growth and a renewed flush of the distinctive speckled flowers.

common_name: Pretty Much Picasso Petunia (Chartreuse-Edged Purple Petunia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Pretty Much Picasso's vigorous, spreading habit fills containers and hanging baskets quickly and needs little deadheading to keep flowering.

directions: Pretty Much Picasso carries hot magenta-purple flowers irregularly bordered in bright chartreuse-green, a bold, artistic hand-painted look that made it one of the most talked-about petunia introductions of its release year and remains a standout in mixed containers. The vigorous, trailing, self-cleaning habit spreads readily over pot edges and needs no deadheading to keep producing new flowers through the season. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, fertilize regularly to sustain its rapid growth, and give it a midsummer trim if the trailing stems become overly long or sparse in the heat, which prompts fresh, bushier regrowth and renewed bloom.

common_name: Supertunia Vista Silverberry Petunia (Vigorous Silvery-Lavender Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; like other Vista series petunias, Silverberry spreads far more vigorously than a standard petunia and needs room to run in a large container or landscape bed.

directions: Supertunia Vista Silverberry produces a soft, silvery lavender-pink flower, a gentler pastel counterpart to the brighter Bubblegum in the same Vista series, on the same extremely vigorous, mounding, trailing plant that can spread three to four feet in a season. Its large scale and heavy bloom production suit big containers, hanging baskets, and mass landscape plantings better than small pots, where it would quickly overwhelm smaller companion plants. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, feed regularly to support its vigorous growth, and shear back by a third to half in midsummer if the planting becomes leggy, which renews compact, floriferous growth for the remainder of the season.

planting.note: Transplant into warm soil after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Archangel was bred for unusually large individual flowers and a well-branched, self-cleaning habit that holds up through the peak heat and humidity of a Gulf South summer.

directions: Archangel produces spikes of unusually large, snapdragon-like flowers along upright, well-branched stems, a bolder-flowered selection than many older angelonia strains, and is largely self-cleaning, dropping spent blooms without leaving behind unsightly dead flowers. Like other angelonia it thrives in the heat and humidity that wilt many summer annuals, blooming continuously from late spring through the first frost with minimal deadheading required. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, water regularly during establishment, and expect strong drought tolerance once the plant is rooted in, making it a reliable performer for Gulf South summer beds and containers.
sources: Pan American Seed / Proven Winners plant introduction notes

common_name: Cora Orchid Vinca (Disease-Resistant Lavender-Orchid Annual Vinca)

planting.note: Transplant into warm soil a week or two after the last frost once nights stay reliably above 60°F; like other Cora selections, Cora Orchid resists the Phytophthora and Aerial Blight diseases that devastate older vinca strains in hot, humid, rainy Gulf South summers.

directions: Cora Orchid carries soft lavender-orchid flowers with the same rounded, five-petaled form as other vinca, standing out among the more common white, pink, and red vinca shades for its cool, unusual pastel tone. It shares the Cora series' strong resistance to soilborne and foliar blight diseases that plague older heirloom vinca strains in wet, humid weather, making it dramatically more reliable in Gulf South plantings that see frequent summer rain. Once established it is remarkably heat- and drought-tolerant, blooming continuously from late spring through the first frost with essentially no deadheading, and its toughness has made the Cora series a standard choice for low-maintenance municipal and home landscape plantings across the Deep South.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Vinca Disease Resistance Trials
